note: Existing-source public educational gallery: CC photos and explicitly credited Bob Harms science/education-only photographs are distinguished. Source labels and arrows are not independent specimen voucher certification.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST
tiles.details: Read the same-species habit and flowering photos in panels 3–6, 10 and 15 (indices 2,3,4,5,9,14). The regional bunch grass bears an open panicle with commonly 2–15 spreading or drooping branches and multiple spikelets along each flowering branch. Panel 3 (index 2) shows a real basal leaf tuft among rock, but roots and their attachment are NOT exposed; DO NOT call this a proved rooted crown. A branch is not a spikelet.
tiles.short: Perennial bunch; ~2–15 long, often spreading one-sided branches
tiles.status: FLOWERING ARCHITECTURE PHOTOGRAPHED — ATTACHED EXPOSED ROOTS MISSING

tiles.heading: 02 · OPEN THE TRUE LEAF COLLAR
tiles.details: See photos 1–2 and 7 (indices 0,1,6). Direct inspection of original pixels shows a green exterior blade–sheath junction and pale collar tissue in photo 1, and Jim Conrad's small junction/lip from Uvalde in photo 7. The true free inner membranous ligule edge, its tiny marginal fringe, and a 1-mm scale are NOT convincingly isolated in these pixels. Fold back the blade and photograph from INSIDE the sheath (adaxial view); never substitute collar hairs or an outside white collar lip.
tiles.short: Short ~0.5–1.5 mm membranous ligule with fringed edge
tiles.status: REAL JUNCTION PHOTOS PRESENT — INNER FRINGED LIGULE WITH SCALE STILL MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · COUNT FLORETS INSIDE ONE SPIKELET
tiles.details: Use Jim Conrad's attached and separated spikelets (panels 8–9, indices 7–8) and Bob Harms' photographed floral-unit series (panels 11–14, indices 10–13) to teach a spikelet versus its internal florets. The published 4–12 mm and 4–13 floret ranges are not measured in these original pixels; capture an intact mature spikelet beside a 1-mm ruler and count the florets within that same spikelet before labeling anatomical counts.

tiles.heading: 04 · EXPOSE THE TWO BASAL GLUMES
tiles.details: Panel 8 shows loose floral units, and the Harms scientific series in panels 11–12 shows detached material (indices 7,10,11), but no verified same-voucher sequence unambiguously labels both basal glumes at millimeter resolution. Published lower and upper glume lengths are references, NOT measurements from these photos. Dissect and show both glumes remaining at the base of a single measured mature spikelet before adding arrows.
tiles.short: Lower ~2.3–4.8 mm; upper ~3.3–6 mm in published key

tiles.heading: 05 · EXAMINE THE BLUNT LEMMA AND LOW SHEATHS
tiles.details: Panel 8 (index 7) shows teased-apart actual Uvalde floral material with blunt-looking tips; panels 11–12 (indices 10–11) supply more Central Texas comparative details. Source references describe a broad, often notched lemma tip; a calibrated individual floret/lemma photo and verified 3-vein count remain missing. Lower, sheath-enclosed cleistogamous spikelets are described in botanical literature but not demonstrated by these images; absence from one sheath proves nothing.
tiles.short: Lemma ~3.5–5 mm, 3-veined, blunt/notched; no long awn
tiles.status: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO — MEASURED LEMMA TIP AND OPTIONAL SHEATH HEAD

tiles.heading: 06 · SEPARATE MUCRONATE SPRANGLETOP
tiles.details: Final panel 16 (index 15) is explicitly Dinebra panicea subsp. mucronata, a DIFFERENT species, shown under its own source determination and individual CC BY-NC terms; don't count it as D. dubium evidence. Compare with same-species head photos 6, 10 and 15 (indices 5,9,14). Green sprangletop is a perennial bunchgrass with larger multiflowered spikelets, while Dinebra species often have smaller annual heads. There is overlap in floret count; confirm true lower growth habit, glumes, lemma and ligule, especially against Diplachne fusca.
tiles.short: Larger usually perennial spikelets vs Dinebra's small annual units
tiles.status: FIELD-READY DIFFERENTIAL; SAME-SCALE LOCAL ANATOMY MISSING

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: GREEN SPRANGLETOP: look for a usually PERENNIAL, often robust bunch with relatively broad bluish-green blades and a terminal head of about 2–15 long slender branches, frequently widely spreading or gently drooping. Branches carry spikelets mostly on ONE side. Then examine ONE mature 4–12 mm spikelet at 10–20×: commonly 4–13 florets (count inside one spikelet), with fairly blunt or NOTCHED, generally awnless or minutely pointed lemmas ~3.5–5 mm long. At the blade–sheath junction verify a SHORT MEMBRANOUS ligule with a fringed margin; in lower sheaths look for optional HIDDEN self-pollinating (cleistogamous) flowers. A flowering-head photo alone cannot prove florets, notches, ligule or hidden heads.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Panels 3 and 10 (indices 2,9): recognize a tuft and whole flowering form, but do not call soil contact actual root anatomy.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: See photos 1–2 and 7 (indices 0,1,6). Direct inspection of original pixels shows a green exterior blade–sheath junction and pale collar tissue in photo 1, and Jim Conrad's small junction/lip from Uvalde in photo 7. The true free inner membranous ligule edge, its tiny marginal fringe, and a 1-mm scale are NOT convincingly isolated in these pixels. Fold back the blade and photograph from INSIDE the sheath (adaxial view); never substitute collar hairs or an outside white collar lip.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Use Jim Conrad's attached and separated spikelets (panels 8–9, indices 7–8) and Bob Harms' photographed floral-unit series (panels 11–14, indices 10–13) to teach a spikelet versus its internal florets. The published 4–12 mm and 4–13 floret ranges are not measured in these original pixels; capture an intact mature spikelet beside a 1-mm ruler and count the florets within that same spikelet before labeling anatomical counts.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: DINEBRA PANICEA subsp. MUCRONATA (mucronate sprangletop): generally a slender ANNUAL with MANY fine ascending branches, tiny ~2–4 mm spikelets with typically 2–4 florets and a much smaller lemma; Green sprangletop is a usually larger PERENNIAL with about 2–15 often widely spreading branches and ~4–12 mm spikelets with 4–13 florets. Both may bear four-flowered spikelets: measure the actual mature spikelet AND inspect rooted habit before deciding. DIPLACHNE FUSCA (bearded sprangletop) can also have long spreading branches; its ligule tends to be much longer and pointed (often ~2–8 mm), and lemma tip shape differs, so confirm with a microscope. Old Leptochloa dubia and Diplachne dubia refer to the same green sprangletop taxon, not new cards. Do not mistake a single branch of the panicle for a whole spikelet.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.

panels.label: 2 · ONE-SIDED SPIKELETS — real green sprangletop, west Texas
panels.caption: Matt Lavin's west-Texas photograph is identified on Wikimedia Commons under the older name Leptochloa dubia. The source specifically describes the upper surface of TWO lateral panicle branches with a SECUND (one-sided) arrangement of spikelets. These are spikelets along branches, not individual florets. Their exact internal floret counts are not certified from the preview.

intro: GREEN SPRANGLETOP: look for a usually PERENNIAL, often robust bunch with relatively broad bluish-green blades and a terminal head of about 2–15 long slender branches, frequently widely spreading or gently drooping. Branches carry spikelets mostly on ONE side. Then examine ONE mature 4–12 mm spikelet at 10–20×: commonly 4–13 florets (count inside one spikelet), with fairly blunt or NOTCHED, generally awnless or minutely pointed lemmas ~3.5–5 mm long. At the blade–sheath junction verify a SHORT MEMBRANOUS ligule with a fringed margin; in lower sheaths look for optional HIDDEN self-pollinating (cleistogamous) flowers. A flowering-head photo alone cannot prove florets, notches, ligule or hidden heads.
memory_rule: PERENNIAL BUNCH + 2–15 OFTEN SPREADING ONE-SIDED BRANCHES + ONE 4–12 mm 4–13-FLORET SPIKELET + BLUNT/NOTCHED LEMMA points to green sprangletop. Dinebra often annual, finer-branched, with ~2–4 mm fewer-flowered spikelets.
safety_note: Image-level CC BY-NC requires genuinely noncommercial site and current license verification; Bob Harms' Selected Monocots permits credited scientific/educational use but the project's recorded scope for LOCAL JPEG copies is not yet reconciled.
field_rule: Keep FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS until actual exposed crown/root attachment and true measured inner ligule are visible on correctly authenticated, individually licensed original photographs.
photo_data_caution: Missing or restricted comparison photographs have not been replaced by guesses. Source statements are not proof the associated structure is visible in any available photo.
comparison_text: DINEBRA PANICEA subsp. MUCRONATA (mucronate sprangletop): generally a slender ANNUAL with MANY fine ascending branches, tiny ~2–4 mm spikelets with typically 2–4 florets and a much smaller lemma; Green sprangletop is a usually larger PERENNIAL with about 2–15 often widely spreading branches and ~4–12 mm spikelets with 4–13 florets. Both may bear four-flowered spikelets: measure the actual mature spikelet AND inspect rooted habit before deciding. DIPLACHNE FUSCA (bearded sprangletop) can also have long spreading branches; its ligule tends to be much longer and pointed (often ~2–8 mm), and lemma tip shape differs, so confirm with a microscope. Old Leptochloa dubia and Diplachne dubia refer to the same green sprangletop taxon, not new cards. Do not mistake a single branch of the panicle for a whole spikelet.
